bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.

- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

# amber

[![Actions Status](https://github.com/dalance/amber/workflows/Regression/badge.svg)](https://github.com/dalance/amber/actions)
[![Crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/amber.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/amber)

**amber** is a code search and replace tool written by [Rust](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
This tool is inspired by [ack](http://beyondgrep.com/),
[ag](https://github.com/ggreer/the_silver_searcher), and other grep-like tools.

## Features

### Useful default settings
- Recursively search from the current directory
- Ignore VCS directories (.git, .hg, .svn, .bzr)
- Ignore binary files
- Output by the colored format

### Multi-threaded searching
Large files ( > 1MB by default) are divided and searched in parallel.

### Interactive replacing
**amber** can replace a keyword over directories (traditionally by `find ... | xargs sed -i '...'`) .
You can decide to do replacing or not interactively.

## Installation

### Arch Linux
Install the `amber-search-git` package from AUR.

```
yay -S amber-search-git
```

### Cargo

You can install with [cargo](https://crates.io/crates/amber).

```
cargo install amber
```

### Manual
Download from [release page](https://github.com/dalance/amber/releases/latest), and extract to the directory in PATH.

## Usage
Two commands (`ambs`/`ambr`) are provided. `ambs` means "amber search", and `ambr` means "amber replace".
The search keyword is not regular expression by default. If you want to use regular expression, add `--regex`.

```
ambs keyword                  // recursively search 'keyword' from the current directory.
ambs keyword path             // recursively search 'keyword' from 'path'.
ambr keyword replacement      // recursively search 'keyword' from the current directory, and replace to 'replacement' interactively.
ambr keyword replacement path // recursively search 'keyword' from 'path', and replace to 'replacement' interactively.
```

**amber** replace interactively by default. If the keyword is found, the following prompt is shown, and wait.
If you input 'y', 'Y', 'Yes', the keyword is replaced. 'a', 'A', 'All' means replacing all keywords non-interactively.

```
Replace keyword? ( Yes[Y], No[N], All[A], Quit[Q] ):
```

If `--regex` option is enabled, regex captures can be used in `replacement` of `ambr`.

```
$ cat text.txt
aaa bbb
$ ambr --no-interactive --regex '(aaa) (?<pat>bbb)' '$1 $pat ${1} ${pat}' test.txt
$ cat text.txt
aaa bbb aaa bbb
```

## Configuration

### Configuration path

You can change configuration by writing a configuration file.
The locations of the configuration file is OS-specific:

 * Linux: `~/.config/amber/ambs.toml`, `/etc/amber/ambs.toml`
 * macOS: `~/Library/Preferences/com.github.dalance.amber/ambs.toml`, `/etc/amber/ambs.toml`
 * Windows: `~/AppData/Roaming/dalance/amber/config/ambs.toml`

For compatibility, if `~/.ambs.toml` exists, it will be preferred to
the OS-specific locations.

The above paths are examples for the configuration of `ambs` command.
`ambr.toml` in the same directory is used for `ambr` command.

### Configurable value

Available entries and default values are below:

```toml
regex          = false
column         = false
row            = false
binary         = false
statistics     = false
skipped        = false
interactive    = true
recursive      = true
symlink        = true
color          = true
file           = true
skip_vcs       = true
skip_gitignore = true
fixed_order    = true
parent_ignore  = true
line_by_match  = false
```

You can choose some entries to override like below:

```toml
column = true
```

## Benchmark

### Environment

- CPU: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Gold 6134 CPU @ 3.20GHz
- MEM: 1.5TB
- OS : CentOS 7.5

### Target Data

- source1: https://github.com/torvalds/linux ( 52998files, 2.2GB )
- source2: https://dumps.wikimedia.org/jawiki/latest/jawiki-latest-pages-articles.xml.bz2 ( 1file, 8.5GB )

### Pattern

- pattern1( many files with many matches ) : 'EXPORT_SYMBOL_GPL' in source1
- pattern2( many files with few matches  ) : 'irq_bypass_register_producer' in source1
- pattern3( a large file with many matches ) : '検索結果' in source2
- pattern4( a large file with few matches  ) : '"Quick Search"' in source2

### Comparison Tools

- amber (v0.5.1)
- [ripgrep](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep) (v0.10.0)
- [grep](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) (v2.20)
- [fastmod](https://github.com/facebookincubator/fastmod) (v0.2.0)
- [find](https://www.gnu.org/software/findutils/)/[sed](https://www.gnu.org/software/sed/) (v4.5.11/v4.2.2)

### Benchmarking Tool

[hyperfine](https://github.com/sharkdp/hyperfine) with the following options.

- `--warmup 3`: to load all data on memory.

### Result

- search ( `compare_ambs.sh` )

| pattern | amber            | ripgrep          | grep             |
| ------- | ---------------- | ---------------- | ---------------- |
| 1       | 212.8ms ( 139% ) | 154.1ms ( 100% ) | 685.2ms ( 448% ) |
| 2       | 199.7ms ( 132% ) | 151.6ms ( 100% ) | 678.7ms ( 448% ) |
| 3       | 1.068s  ( 100% ) | 4.642s  ( 434% ) | 3.869s  ( 362% ) |
| 4       | 1.027s  ( 100% ) | 4.409s  ( 429% ) | 3.118s  ( 304% ) |

- replace ( `compare_ambr.sh` )

| pattern | amber            | fastmod          | find/sed            |
| ------- | ---------------- | ---------------- | ------------------- |
| 1       | 792.2ms ( 100% ) | 1231ms  ( 155% ) | 155724ms ( 19657% ) |
| 2       | 418.1ms ( 119% ) | 352.4ms ( 100% ) | 157396ms ( 44663% ) |
| 3       | 18.390s ( 100% ) | 74.282s ( 404% ) | 639.740s ( 3479% )  |
| 4       | 17.777s ( 100% ) | 74.204s ( 417% ) | 625.756s ( 3520% )  |
</output>

## Usage
Two commands (`ambs`/`ambr`) are provided. `ambs` means "amber search", and `ambr` means "amber replace".
The search keyword is not regular expression by default. If you want to use regular expression, add `--regex`.

```
ambs keyword                  // recursively search 'keyword' from the current directory.
ambs keyword path             // recursively search 'keyword' from 'path'.
ambr keyword replacement      // recursively search 'keyword' from the current directory, and replace to 'replacement' interactively.
ambr keyword replacement path // recursively search 'keyword' from 'path', and replace to 'replacement' interactively.
```

**amber** replace interactively by default. If the keyword is found, the following prompt is shown, and wait.
If you input 'y', 'Y', 'Yes', the keyword is replaced. 'a', 'A', 'All' means replacing all keywords non-interactively.

```
Replace keyword? ( Yes[Y], No[N], All[A], Quit[Q] ):
```

If `--regex` option is enabled, regex captures can be used in `replacement` of `ambr`.

```
$ cat text.txt
aaa bbb
$ ambr --no-interactive --regex '(aaa) (?<pat>bbb)' '$1 $pat ${1} ${pat}' test.txt
$ cat text.txt
aaa bbb aaa bbb
```

## Configuration

### Configuration path

You can change configuration by writing a configuration file.
The locations of the configuration file is OS-specific:

 * Linux: `~/.config/amber/ambs.toml`, `/etc/amber/ambs.toml`
 * macOS: `~/Library/Preferences/com.github.dalance.amber/ambs.toml`, `/etc/amber/ambs.toml`
 * Windows: `~/AppData/Roaming/dalance/amber/config/ambs.toml`

For compatibility, if `~/.ambs.toml` exists, it will be preferred to
the OS-specific locations.

The above paths are examples for the configuration of `ambs` command.
`ambr.toml` in the same directory is used for `ambr` command.

### Configurable value

Available entries and default values are below:

```toml
regex          = false
column         = false
row            = false
binary         = false
statistics     = false
skipped        = false
interactive    = true
recursive      = true
symlink        = true
color          = true
file           = true
skip_vcs       = true
skip_gitignore = true
fixed_order    = true
parent_ignore  = true
line_by_match  = false
```

You can choose some entries to override like below:

```toml
column = true
```

## Benchmark

### Environment

- CPU: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Gold 6134 CPU @ 3.20GHz
- MEM: 1.5TB
- OS : CentOS 7.5

### Target Data

- source1: https://github.com/torvalds/linux ( 52998files, 2.2GB )
- source2: https://dumps.wikimedia.org/jawiki/latest/jawiki-latest-pages-articles.xml.bz2 ( 1file, 8.5GB )

### Pattern

- pattern1( many files with many matches ) : 'EXPORT_SYMBOL_GPL' in source1
- pattern2( many files with few matches  ) : 'irq_bypass_register_producer' in source1
- pattern3( a large file with many matches ) : '検索結果' in source2
- pattern4( a large file with few matches  ) : '"Quick Search"' in source2

### Comparison Tools

- amber (v0.5.1)
- [ripgrep](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep) (v0.10.0)
- [grep](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) (v2.20)

# Summary of output format:
# - With file, no row/col: "filename: content\n{spaces}-> replacement"
#   - spaces count = len("filename: ") - 3
# - With file, row:col: "filename: row:col:content\n{spaces}-> replacement"  
#   - spaces count = len("filename: row:col:") - 3
# - Without file, no row/col: "    content\n -> replacement"
#   - 4 spaces before content, 1 space + "-> " before replacement
# - Without file, row:col: "row:col:content\n  -> replacement"
#   - No prefix before content row/col, spaces = len("row:col:") - 3

# Hmm wait, let me recheck the no-file, no row/col case:
# "    test content hello" -> 4 spaces
# " -> test content goodbye" -> 1 space then "-> "
# Total prefix = 4
# Arrow prefix = 1 + 2 = 3 = "-> "... that's wrong

# Actually the arrow line is " -> " which is 4 chars too:
# " " + "-" + ">" + " " = 4

# So the rule is: both lines have the same width prefix before the content/replacement
# with the prefix being "filename: " (with file) or "    " (4 spaces, without file, no row/col)
# or "row:col:" (without file, with row/col) or "filename: row:col:" (with both)

# And the "-> " indicator is aligned to the right within the prefix, i.e., placed at 
# prefix_len - 3 spaces from the left, then "-> " takes 3 chars

# Let me verify the " -> " interpretation for no-file case:
python3 -c "
line1_prefix = '    '  # 4 spaces
line2_prefix = ' -> '  # 1 space + '-> ' = 4 chars
print(f'line1_prefix = {repr(line1_prefix)}, len={len(line1_prefix)}')
print(f'line2_prefix = {repr(line2_prefix)}, len={len(line2_prefix)}')
"

# which gives 20 on this system.

# The statistics output shows thread timing data, but does it affect correctness of search/replace?
# NO! The thread count only affects PERFORMANCE and the STATISTICS output.
# The functional behavior (which files are replaced, what output is shown) doesn't depend on thread count.

# So for our implementation:
# - We can use available_parallelism() for thread count
# - The statistics will show different thread counts on different systems
# - But the functional behavior will be identical

# Go is available! Go has:
# - regexp standard library
# - os, path/filepath for file walking
# - fmt for output
# - bufio for reading
# Go would be a good choice!

# But wait - let me think about the amber features more carefully:
# The regex flavor in amber is likely Rust's regex crate which uses RE2 syntax
# (no backreferences/lookaheads). Go's regexp is also RE2-based!

# Let me start implementing in Go.
# Features I need:
# 1. CLI parsing (flag package)
# 2. Recursive file walking (filepath.Walk)
# 3. Binary file detection
# 4. VCS directory skipping
# 5. .gitignore handling
# 6. Pattern matching (plain text and regex)
# 7. Interactive replacement
# 8. Color output (ANSI codes)
# 9. Concurrent file processing
# 10. Statistics output
# 11. Config file support

# But wait - Go's regex syntax is different from Rust's regex.
# Rust regex: named captures are (?P<name>...) or (?<name>...)
# Go regex: named captures are (?P<name>...)
# The replacement in Rust regex uses $1, ${1}, $name, ${name}
# Go regex replacement uses ${1}, ${name} format
# So there are differences to handle

# Let me first understand all the features thoroughly before implementing

# Test the preserve-time option
echo "hello world" > /tmp/testdir/file1.txt
touch -t 202001010000 /tmp/testdir/file1.txt
ls -la /tmp/testdir/file1.txt

tmux send-keys -t test_amber "ls -la /tmp/testdir/file1.txt" Enter
sleep 1
tmux capture-pane -t test_amber -p | tail -3

# With TERM=xterm: colors work, "n" input is accepted!
# The ANSI reset at the end is "\x1b(B\x1b[m\x1b(B\x1b[m"
# vs in tmux: "\x1b[m\x0f\x1b[m\x0f"
# The difference is the terminal type's reset sequence.

# Actually wait - let me check the color codes in the terminfo database
# "SGR 0" in xterm is "\x1b(B\x1b[m" (set charset to ASCII B, then set SGR to 0)
# While in "screen" terminal (tmux), it's "\x1b[m\x0f" (SGR reset + SI shift-in)

# So the terminfo reset_all sequence differs between terminal types!
# This is actually the termcolor crate's behavior - it uses terminfo to output color.

# The amber binary uses the termcolor crate (or similar) which reads TERM to output correct sequences.
# This is important for our implementation!

# Now I understand the exit code issue:
# - When TERM is not set: exit code 1 (no-op mode)
# - When TERM is set: exit code 0 (normal operation)

# Let me verify with no TERM variable
echo "hello world" > /tmp/testdir/file1.txt
unset TERM && /workspace/executable --no-interactive 'hello' 'goodbye' /tmp/testdir/file1.txt
echo "Exit: $?"
cat /tmp/testdir/file1.txt

# TERM="" : exit 1, NO replacement
# TERM=dumb: exit 1, replacement HAPPENS
# 
# This is the key difference. The amber binary uses the termcolor crate which has two modes:
# 1. When TERM is empty/not set: termcolor can't detect terminal, so it outputs nothing.
#    The program fails to write any output, and since the "display match" function fails early,
#    the replacement doesn't happen either.
# 2. When TERM=dumb: termcolor detects "dumb" terminal, writes empty/plain output (no colors),
#    but the write itself succeeds. The program proceeds with replacement.
#    But the exit code is 1 because... the termcolor "reset all" at the end fails? Or because
#    the color mode is "disabled" and some flag is set.

# Actually, I wonder if the exit code for TERM=dumb is from a specific write failure.
# Let me check what the output looks like with TERM=dumb redirected to a file:

echo "hello world" > /tmp/testdir/file1.txt
TERM=dumb /workspace/executable --no-interactive 'hello' 'goodbye' /tmp/testdir/file1.txt > /tmp/dumb_cap.txt 2>&1
python3 -c "
with open('/tmp/dumb_cap.txt', 'rb') as f:
    data = f.read()
print(f'Output length: {len(data)}')
print(f'Output: {repr(data)}')
"

# With TERM=dumb in tmux: no display output visible on terminal, exit 1, file replaced.
# The program silently does replacements with TERM=dumb.

# Now let me understand the actual behavior properly.
# The amber binary behavior based on TERM:
# 1. TERM not set or empty: NO-OP mode - exits 1, doesn't replace, doesn't output
# 2. TERM=dumb: SILENT mode - exits 1, replaces files, no output  
# 3. TERM=anything_else: NORMAL mode - exits 0, replaces files, shows colored output

# For our implementation, this distinction is important.
# The "dumb" mode means the termcolor crate's "ColorChoice::Auto" is set,
# it detects TERM=dumb and disables colors, but still proceeds with the operation.
# The exit code 1 for TERM=dumb is likely because the termcolor reset-all writes nothing
# and the program returns an error from there.

# Actually - I think for the purposes of our implementation, the exact TERM=dumb behavior
# is edge case. Let me focus on the normal behavior which is what users actually see.

# Let me now start implementing the amber binary in Go.
# I'll need to figure out the threading model from scratch.

# Key features to implement:
# 1. CLI argument parsing (flag package or manual)
# 2. Recursive file walking with filters (VCS dirs, gitignore, binary detection)
# 3. Pattern matching (plain text and regex)
# 4. Match display with alignment
# 5. Interactive replacement prompt
# 6. Non-interactive replacement
# 7. Color output using termcolor-like logic
# 8. Statistics output
# 9. Temp file based atomic replacement
# 10. Multiple threads for matching

# Let me start coding!
mkdir -p /workspace/src
cd /workspace

# Initialize go module
cat > /workspace/go.mod << 'EOF'
module amber

go 1.21
EOF

echo "Project structure created"

# The program reads 'y' from stdin pipe, then falls back to /dev/tty
# In our background test (& at end), /dev/tty is the terminal which receives spaces
# The infinite loop shows it's continuously reading from /dev/tty getting empty chars

# Key behavior confirmed:
# 1. Reads one char at a time from stdin
# 2. When stdin is exhausted (EOF), opens /dev/tty and reads from there
# 3. If /dev/tty also returns empty (non-blocking?), it re-prompts infinitely

# For our implementation:
# - Read from stdin first
# - On EOF, try to open /dev/tty
# - Read one char at a time

# Actually the infinite space reading might be a special behavior when /dev/tty returns 0 bytes
# (non-blocking read?) In our case, running in background means /dev/tty is the bash terminal
# that's running other commands.

# Let me kill that background job
kill $(jobs -p) 2>/dev/null || true
tmux send-keys -t test_amber "" ""
sleep 1

# Now let me understand the complete implementation requirements:
# 
# 1. The input reading mechanism:
#    - Open /dev/tty for input (NOT stdin)
#    - Read one character at a time (raw mode)
#    - This ensures it works even when stdin is redirected
#    - The piped "echo y | ..." worked because it falls through to /dev/tty
#
# Wait... but "echo y |" worked! If the program uses /dev/tty only, piped input would be ignored.
# Let me re-test:

echo "hello world" > /tmp/testdir/file1.txt
printf "y" | TERM=screen /workspace/executable 'hello' 'goodbye' /tmp/testdir/file1.txt > /tmp/tty_test.txt 2>&1
echo "Exit: $?"
cat /tmp/testdir/file1.txt

# YES! Piping 'y' to stdin (not to /dev/tty) DOES work!
# The program reads from stdin when available.
# And falls back to /dev/tty when stdin is exhausted.

# Wait - in our run above, piping 'y' to stdin and stdout redirected...
# The program would normally open /dev/tty for interactive input (a common pattern),
# but since stdin has data, it reads that first.

# Actually the most likely implementation is:
# - Uses a Rust "console" or custom TTY reader that reads from /dev/tty
# - But /dev/tty IS the current terminal (same as stdin when running interactively)
# - When stdin is a pipe, /dev/tty is still the terminal, not the pipe

# But piped 'y' works! This means the program DOES read from stdin.
# Maybe it uses stdin directly but in raw mode (one char at a time)?

# Let me check if reading from /dev/tty vs stdin makes a difference:
# Create a test where stdin has 'y' but /dev/tty would give 'n'
# This is hard to test without two terminals...

# Let me just accept the behavior: the program reads from stdin in raw mode.
# When stdin is a TTY: raw mode, one char at a time.  
# When stdin is a pipe: reads from pipe.
# When pipe is exhausted: continues prompting (infinite loop on /dev/tty or hangs)

# Actually looking at it more carefully - the Rust "console" crate reads from /dev/tty directly.
# When we pipe 'y', it goes to stdin. But if the program reads from /dev/tty...
# Let me test by redirecting /dev/tty explicitly:

echo "hello world" > /tmp/testdir/file1.txt
TERM=screen /workspace/executable 'hello' 'goodbye' /tmp/testdir/file1.txt < /dev/null > /tmp/null_test.txt 2>&1 &
sleep 2
head -5 /tmp/null_test.txt
kill $(jobs -p) 2>/dev/null || true

# Actually I think I understand now:
# - The termcolor crate's "ColorSpec" (for color styles) when TERM=dumb: outputs empty
# - The main text (non-colored) is output via println which always works
# - The "reset all" command via termcolor fails for TERM=dumb -> error -> exit 1

# Let me rethink the dumb terminal behavior:
# With TERM=dumb:
# - Plain text output IS shown (file path, content, prompt, response)
# - No color codes are emitted for the colored parts (before, match, after)
# - The final reset (termcolor flush) fails -> exit 1
# - File IS replaced

# This means:

# 2. At the end, try to flush/reset the termcolor stream

orig_stripped = strip_timing(re.sub(r'\x1b\[[^m]*m', '', orig).replace('\x0f', ''))

print('Stats format match:', my_stripped == orig_stripped)
if my_stripped != orig_stripped:
    print('MY:')
    print(my_stripped)
    print('OR:')
    print(orig_stripped)
"

# 1. Statistics goes to STDERR (not stdout)!
# 2. The timing format: "0s / 0.000276908s" (two values: busy/total)
# 3. The busy is "0s" (because threads waited, not busy running)
# 4. Match threads: 8 (Match00-Match07)
# 5. The statistics are in CYAN color on stderr

# Wait - I also need to understand the timing format better.
# "0s" vs "0.000276908s"
# The "0s" is displayed when busy time is zero (or very small)
# The actual format looks like: busy value / total value
# where busy = actual CPU time used by thread
# and total = elapsed wall clock time

# For our implementation, since we're using goroutines, 
# we need to track total elapsed time per thread (the easy part)
# and "busy" time (harder - approximated as actual work time)
# 
# For simplicity, let me use elapsed time for both (they'll be the same).
# The key is to output the correct FORMAT.

# Looking at the timing output more carefully:
# "0s / 0.000276908s"
# - "0s" = 0 seconds (busy time = 0)
# - "0.000276908s" = 0.276908 milliseconds (total time)
# 
# When busy=0: "0s" (no decimal, just "0s")
# When busy>0: probably shows in seconds with decimals
# 
# My current fmtDur function:
# - 0 -> "0s"
# - <1s -> fmt.Sprintf("%gs", secs) where secs = ns/1e9
# Let me check if "%g" gives the right format:

python3 -c "
# Check Go's %g format for various values
import math
tests = [0.000276908, 0.000301031, 0.000584814]
for t in tests:
    g = '%g' % t
    print(f'{t} -> %g: {g}')
    # Also check scientific notation
    print(f'  vs: {t:.9f}s')
"

# Statistics are printed AFTER finalReset(). But finalReset writes the reset to stderr.
# Then printStatistics writes to stderrWriter (same buffer).
# The issue is the order of writes:
# 1. finalReset: writes reset to stderrWriter, then flushes stderrWriter
# 2. printStatistics: writes stats to stderrWriter (starts fresh buffer after flush)
# 
# But the stderrWriter was flushed in finalReset, so the stats would be written after the reset!
# The output would be: reset + stats
# But the original has: stats + reset
# 
# I need to:
# 1. Print statistics BEFORE final reset
# 2. Then write final reset

# Let me look at the original order:
# In the original amber:
# 1. Print statistics (including "\n\n" at end)
# 2. Write final reset (as part of stream cleanup/drop)
# 
# So the order should be: stats THEN reset.
# Let me swap the order:

python3 << 'PYEOF'
with open('/workspace/main.go', 'r') as f:
    content = f.read()

# Find and swap the order
old = '''	// Final resets
	finalReset()
	
	// Print statistics
	if cfg.Statistics {
		printStatistics(cfg)
	}'''

new = '''	// Print statistics (before final reset)
	if cfg.Statistics {
		printStatistics(cfg)
	}
	
	// Final resets
	finalReset()'''

if old in content:
    content = content.replace(old, new)
    print("Swapped order")
else:
    print("Pattern not found!")

with open('/workspace/main.go', 'w') as f:
    f.write(content)

run_test() {
    local desc="$1"
    local term="${2:-screen}"
    local setup_cmd="$3"
    local test_cmd_suffix="$4"
    local input="$5"

    local my_exit=$?
    
    eval "$setup_cmd"
    printf "$input" | TERM=$term /workspace/executable $test_cmd_suffix > /tmp/orig.txt 2>/tmp/orig.err
    local orig_exit=$?
    
    stdout_match=true
    stderr_match=true
    exit_match=true
    diff -q /tmp/my.txt /tmp/orig.txt > /dev/null || stdout_match=false
    diff -q /tmp/my.err /tmp/orig.err > /dev/null || stderr_match=false
    [ $my_exit -eq $orig_exit ] || exit_match=false
    
    if $stdout_match && $stderr_match && $exit_match; then
        echo "PASS: $desc"
    else
        echo "FAIL: $desc (stdout=$stdout_match stderr=$stderr_match exit=$exit_match [my=$my_exit orig=$orig_exit])"
    fi
}

printf "" | TERM=screen /workspace/executable --version > /tmp/orig_ver.txt 2>&1
if diff -q /tmp/my_ver.txt /tmp/orig_ver.txt > /dev/null; then echo "PASS: version"; else echo "FAIL: version"; cat /tmp/my_ver.txt; cat /tmp/orig_ver.txt; fi

import subprocess, os, tempfile

def run(cmd, inp="", term="screen"):
    env = os.environ.copy()
    if term: env['TERM'] = term
    else: env.pop('TERM', None)
    r = subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, input=inp.encode(), capture_output=True, env=env)
    return r.returncode, r.stdout, r.stderr

tests_passed = 0
tests_failed = 0

def check(desc, setup, args, inp="", term="screen"):
    global tests_passed, tests_failed
    subprocess.run(setup, shell=True, capture_output=True)
    mc, mo, me = run(f"/workspace/executable {args}", inp, term)
    subprocess.run(setup, shell=True, capture_output=True)
    oc, oo, oe = run(f"/tmp/amber_test {args}", inp, term)
    
    if mo==oo and me==oe and mc==oc:
        tests_passed += 1
        print(f"  PASS: {desc}")
    else:
        tests_failed += 1
        print(f"  FAIL: {desc} (exit: exe={mc} test={oc})")
        if mo!=oo: print(f"    Stdout exe: {repr(mo[:100])}\n    Stdout tst: {repr(oo[:100])}")
        if me!=oe: print(f"    Stderr exe: {repr(me[:100])}\n    Stderr tst: {repr(oe[:100])}")

print("=== Core Functionality ===")
check("no-TERM exit1", "echo hi > /tmp/t.txt", "--no-interactive 'hi' 'bye' /tmp/t.txt", "", None)
check("basic replace nocolor", "echo 'hello' > /tmp/t.txt", "--no-interactive --no-color 'hello' 'bye' /tmp/t.txt")
check("basic replace color", "echo 'hello' > /tmp/t.txt", "--no-interactive 'hello' 'bye' /tmp/t.txt")
check("interactive y", "echo 'hello' > /tmp/t.txt", "'hello' 'bye' /tmp/t.txt", "y")
check("interactive n", "echo 'hello' > /tmp/t.txt", "'hello' 'bye' /tmp/t.txt", "n")
check("interactive q", "echo 'hello' > /tmp/t.txt", "'hello' 'bye' /tmp/t.txt", "q")
check("interactive a (2 files)", "echo 'hello' > /tmp/t1.txt; echo 'hello' > /tmp/t2.txt", "'hello' 'bye' /tmp/t1.txt /tmp/t2.txt", "a")

print("\n=== Terminal Types ===")
check("TERM=xterm", "echo 'hello' > /tmp/t.txt", "--no-interactive 'hello' 'bye' /tmp/t.txt", "", "xterm")
check("TERM=dumb", "echo 'hello' > /tmp/t.txt", "--no-interactive 'hello' 'bye' /tmp/t.txt", "", "dumb")
check("TERM=dumb --no-color", "echo 'hello' > /tmp/t.txt", "--no-interactive --no-color 'hello' 'bye' /tmp/t.txt", "y", "dumb")

print("\n=== Output Format ===")
check("--row --column", "echo 'XXX hello YYY' > /tmp/t.txt", "--row --column 'hello' 'bye' /tmp/t.txt", "n")
check("--no-file", "echo 'hello world' > /tmp/t.txt", "--no-file 'hello' 'bye' /tmp/t.txt", "n")
check("--no-file --row --column", "echo 'XXX hello YYY' > /tmp/t.txt", "--no-file --row --column 'hello' 'bye' /tmp/t.txt", "n")

print("\n=== File Handling ===")
check("binary skip", "printf '\\x00\\x01hello' > /tmp/b.bin", "--no-interactive --skipped 'hello' 'bye' /tmp/b.bin")
check("binary enable", "printf '\\x00\\x01hello' > /tmp/b.bin", "--no-interactive --binary 'hello' 'bye' /tmp/b.bin")
check("preserve-time", "echo 'hello' > /tmp/t.txt && touch -t 202001010000 /tmp/t.txt", "--no-interactive --preserve-time 'hello' 'bye' /tmp/t.txt")
check("no-recursive", "mkdir -p /tmp/td/sub; echo 'hi' > /tmp/td/f.txt; echo 'hi' > /tmp/td/sub/f.txt", "--no-interactive --no-color --no-recursive 'hi' 'bye' /tmp/td")

print("\n=== Regex ===")
check("basic regex", "echo 'aaa bbb' > /tmp/t.txt", "--no-interactive --regex '(aaa)' 'X${1}X' /tmp/t.txt")
check("named groups", "echo 'aaa bbb' > /tmp/t.txt", "--no-interactive --regex '(aaa) (?P<pat>bbb)' '${1} ${pat}' /tmp/t.txt")

print(f"\n=== Summary: {tests_passed}/{tests_passed+tests_failed} passed ===")
PYEOF
